title: Lazica
capsule: Lazica (Egrisi in Georgian) was a kingdom on the eastern Black Sea littoral in western Georgia that emerged in the 2nd–3rd centuries CE from the breakup of the older kingdom of Colchis, of which it is regarded as the successor. Centered on the port of Phasis (modern Poti) and the fortress of Archaeopolis, it became a strategically vital client of Rome and later Byzantium, with Christianity established as the state religion in the early 6th century under King Tzath I. Its position made it a contested buffer between the Byzantine and Sasanian empires, and the defection of King Gubazes II from Persia to Byzantium triggered the protracted Lazic War (541–562). The kingdom remained a Byzantine-aligned domain until its last ruler acknowledged Arab suzerainty around 697.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The kingdom's general territory along the eastern Black Sea coast is established by Byzantine and Persian sources; precise interior boundaries are difficult to map given the mountainous terrain and clientage relationships that made frontiers fluid.
